To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we used family-based genome sequencing to: identify the gene causing Miller syndrome, identify the causative genes for a recessive disorder in both children of a family, identify a very high percentage of sequencing errors, and estimate a human intergeneration genome mutation rate.
Whole-genome sequencing of a family quartet, consisting of two affected siblings and their parents, allowed us to identify the genetic causes of their two recessive disorders.

(a) family-based whole-genome sequencing is a powerful tool for identifying rare recessive disorders, (b) the mutation rate in the human genome is about 1.1 × 10(-8), and (c) the accuracy of whole-genome sequencing can be improved to > 99.99%.

the development of novel computational methods for the analysis of genome sequence data.
the development of a new method for analyzing the human genome.
the identification of genes responsible for human genetic disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genome sequence of a single individual, in the absence of a family history of genetic disease, is insufficient to make a definitive diagnosis of a genetic disease.
whole-genome sequencing of a family quartet is an effective method for identifying causative genes in a Mendelian disorder and is a powerful approach for understanding human genetic variation.

the genome is not just a collection of genes, but also a collection of variants that can be used to identify genes that cause disease.

The main takeaway from our work is that
family-based genome sequencing can be used to identify causative genes for Mendelian disorders, even when the disorder is rare.
family-based sequencing is a very powerful tool for genetic analysis.
whole-genome sequencing of a family quartet is an efficient way to identify rare variants in Mendelian disorders, and it is an excellent way to estimate the mutation rate in humans.
